title: Survival up. Did anyone live longer?
hook: A new test makes more people alive 5 years after diagnosis. Does that mean longer lives?

doesNotKnow: that the survival clock starts at diagnosis, so finding an illness earlier raises this count even when nobody lives a day longer (lead time)

misconception: If more people are alive 5 years after diagnosis, they must be living longer.
objective: The learner can explain that in a group of 14 whose deaths do not move, finding the illness 3 years earlier raises 'alive 5 years after diagnosis' from 6 to 12 because only the start of the clock moved (lead time), and that comparing deaths in whole groups is not fooled by this.

claims.text: In the model, with no test 6 of 14 (43%) are alive 5 years after diagnosis; with the test finding the illness 3 years earlier, 12 of 14 (86%), with every death on the same day.
Finding an illness earlier raises survival counted from diagnosis even when nobody lives longer; this is called lead time. Only the start of the clock moves.
claims.source: Definition of lead time: survival is measured from diagnosis, so moving diagnosis earlier while death is fixed lengthens measured survival by construction.

claims.text: To judge an earlier test, compare deaths in whole groups.
claims.source: In the model, death dates do not depend on the test, so deaths per group are unaffected by when diagnosis happens. Optional context, not on the card: Welch, Schwartz and Woloshin 2000, JAMA 283(22). Unverified: needs a human source check including the citation.

claims.text: 14 people with a made-up illness, found when symptoms start, each dying 1 to 8 years later; treatment changes nothing. This toy makes no claim about any real test.
claims.source: Invented model (brief), stated on the stage, in the question and in the reveal. No advice about screening.

recall.question: A clinic starts a scan that finds a disease 2 years sooner. Its 5-year survival jumps. What is the fair way to tell whether the scan helps?
options: Compare death rates in whole scanned and unscanned groups
Count how many more cases the scan finds
recall.why: Survival counted from diagnosis rises whenever diagnosis moves earlier, even if no death moves; deaths in whole groups do not depend on when diagnosis happened.
